To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

protein migration from transplated nucleus in Amoeba involves two classes of proteins, one with a MW range of 9,000-110,000 D, and a pI range of 7.0-7.6, which is involved with RNA transport; the second class has MW range of 11,000-45,000 D, pI range of about 5.9-7.0, and exhibits shuttling character.
the migratory proteins are a class of proteins which are shuttling between the nucleus and cytoplasm, and which may be involved in the nucleocytoploplasmic transfer of RNAs.

The migratory proteins from transplanted Amoeba nuclei have a range of pIs between 7. 0 and 7 6, and a MW range between 9 000 and 110 000 D, while the shuttling migratory proteins have pIs between 6.0 and 6.9 and MWs of 11 000 to 45 000D.

the nucleocytoplasminic transfer of macromolecules, which is a fundamental aspect of the regulation of gene expression.
the nucleocyoplasmic transfer of proteins in Amoeba.
a nuclear protein transfer system which appears to be involved with a nucleocytoplasm RNA shuttle mechanism.

the migratory proteins are heterogeneous, and that their function is not clear.
the migratory proteins are involved in the regulation of the nuclear RNA synthesis and the shuttling of proteins between the cytoplasm and nucleus.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a nucleus transplated into a host amoebal cell is able to regulate the host's metabolism and growth, by the transfer of nuclear RNA and cytoplasmic proteins to the cytoplasm.
the migratory nuclear proteins are involved in RNA transfer and cytoplasmic regulation.
the nucleus of A. proteus contains two classes of migratory proteins.

protein migration into the cytoplasm from a transplanted nucleus is a dynamic and regulated process.
